findings.where: Hero, first screen (desktop and phone), and the style tile as a whole
findings.fault: Mark himself doesn't appear anywhere: there is no portrait and no place for one, not even a captioned stand-in. The palette rule 'three colours with hard edges and no blending' also leaves no visible way for a photograph or video of him to sit in this look. A large drawing of the arches holds the first screen where a person would be.
findings.who_objects: Mark and the founder, choosing between the five directions. Client value 3 ('the man himself — Mark is seen') and value 8 (video welcome) are lines every tile must answer. This tile gives them no way to judge how a real face or film would sit on the granite, and the strict three-colour rule suggests it wouldn't. A development-bank officer visiting a solo advisor's site expects to see who they would be hiring (first-visit trust item 1).

findings.where: Hero, the line under the name ('Advice on infrastructure projects… from a former Lead Lawyer in the World Bank's PPP Group')
findings.fault: The first screen talks about Mark in the third person, under a two-line inscribed title. Nowhere on it does Mark speak in his own words. The whole screen reads like a carved plaque or an institution's nameboard, not a person you can approach.
findings.who_objects: Mark, whose brand sheet §5 asks for a personal, approachable advisor whose individual voice is the brand, never a firm's voice. Value 3 asks for him to be 'heard, in his own words'. The only first-person line on the page is buried in the article specimen.

findings.where: Hero, the five-second read: the heading and the line under it
findings.fault: The first screen says what Mark does but not who it's for or where he works. Development agencies and the countries or regions of his work are both missing, so a visitor can't tell at a glance whether this advisor fits their mandate.
findings.who_objects: The audience in brand sheet §1: development-bank and agency staff looking for an advisor. They screen candidates by the type of client and the region before reading further (first-visit trust items 2 and 6, 'What a visitor must be sure of': work for organisations like theirs, in their region).

findings.where: Hero heading, 'MARK · M · MOSELEY / INFRASTRUCTURE · ADVISOR' (desktop; on phone the role takes two of the three lines)
findings.fault: The role line is the same size and weight as the name and is wider, so on a squint the generic title 'Infrastructure Advisor' outweighs Mark's name. Nothing in the hero ranks the person above the job title.
findings.who_objects: Mark: the brand sheet makes the individual the brand (§5, value 1). A heading where the job title wins reads like a firm's category label, not a named person.

findings.where: Texture tile (the joint-line diagram with the red 'M') and the page ground
findings.fault: The direction's whole idea is the aqueduct's own dressed grey stone, but stone appears only as a small line diagram in a captioned box. Everywhere else the page is a flat grey field. Seen as a page, v3 reads as plain grey paper with red accents, not as stone, so its one signature isn't felt.
findings.who_objects: The founder and Mark, comparing five directions to pick a look. They can't judge whether a stone ground carries the site when the tile never puts the stone under any content. The layout and animation rounds would inherit an untested idea.

findings.where: Article specimen, the title 'THE WORLD'S BEST PUBLIC-PRIVATE PARTNERSHIP LAW', against the type rule 'headings… always in capitals, always tracked'
findings.fault: A short title already fills three lines of tracked carved capitals. Mark's real titles run longer: the lecture listed right below, 'Streamlining the PPP Process: Meeting the 'Abundance' Challenge', is set in the sans, so the tile never shows a long title in the heading face. Under the rule, every post Angélique adds would open with a dense block of capitals, four or five lines of them.
findings.who_objects: Angélique and Mark's readers. Value 9 asks that every part of the look survive a lay editor adding a post. Readers on article pages (Read mode) face a slab of all-caps before the first sentence.

findings.where: Motion sketch, the note under the timeline table ('…(#13, docs/research/animation-length.md F5/F12)…') and the code-styled 'cubic-bezier(0.5, 0, 0.2, 1)'
findings.fault: Internal ticket numbers, a repository file path and raw CSS sit in the client-facing tile in a monospace third face. They read as build notes and make an otherwise calm section look busy and technical.
findings.who_objects: Mark, who will see this tile. He finds busyness off-putting (§6), and file paths and ticket numbers mean nothing to him. They make the identity look like a working document rather than a look to choose.
